transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, it’s a bit hard to explain, but I guess I’m here because... well, people have been telling me they can’t follow what I’m saying anymore. I’m an artist, you see, and normally I’m very good at communicating my vision. I know how to write, I know how to present my work. But lately, when I sit down to write my artist statements, or even when I’m just jotting down routine client notes for a commission, it all gets completely tangled up. 

Like, I’ll be in a meeting with a client or a gallery rep, and I’ll start out talking about the physical piece—the textures of the canvas, the way the light hits the impasto, just normal artistic things. But then, before I know it, I’m jumping straight from the textures into the financial budgets, and then somehow the budget numbers are deeply connected to these secret meanings I’ve been noticing in the world, like the numbers are tied to the colors and the universe's underlying geometry. And I just keep jumping from one thing to the next, from the paint to the money to the hidden messages. 

To me, it makes perfect, absolute sense in the moment. The connections are all right there, vividly right in front of me! But everyone just looks at me with these blank, confused expressions. They keep stopping me, interrupting my flow, and telling me they have absolutely no idea what I’m trying to explain. It’s incredibly frustrating because I have so much I need to convey, but the words just sort of spill out in this massive, interconnected web that apparently no one else can untangle. So, I guess that's why I'm here.
Do you find that your thoughts and ability to explain things become more tangled or disconnected when you're feeling anxious, upset, or stressed?

Well, um... I don't really think so? I mean, I know people always assume that when you can't get your words out right, it must be because you're having a panic attack or you're under some massive deadline, but for me, that's not really it at all. I actually haven't noticed it being tied to being upset or anxious. In fact, sometimes it happens when I'm feeling absolutely wonderful, completely calm and centered. 

Like, just last week, I was having this incredibly peaceful morning. I had just brewed my coffee—I use this specific pour-over method because the circular motion of pouring the water really helps me ground myself before I start painting for the day—and I was sitting by the window in my studio. The light was coming in, hitting the dust motes, and I felt completely at ease. Zero stress. I wasn't upset about anything. But then my studio manager walked in to ask a really simple question about ordering more gesso, and I opened my mouth to say yes, but instead I started explaining how the white of the gesso was actually absorbing the financial energy of the room, and how the invoice numbers were dictating the brush strokes I was going to use later that afternoon. 

I wasn't stressed at all when she walked in! I was perfectly happy. But she still gave me that same look, that completely lost expression, like I was speaking a foreign language. And I kept trying to explain it to her, breaking down the exact relationship between the pigment density and the bank account routing numbers, because it was so clear to me, but she just sort of slowly backed out of the room. So, no, it’s not really about being upset or pressured. It just... it just happens. Whether I'm stressed or completely relaxed, the connections are just always there, demanding to be explained, and the words just weave together on their own. It doesn't seem to matter how I'm feeling emotionally at the time, the web just keeps spinning itself.
Do you ever see or hear things that other people do not?

Well... yes, actually. I mean, it’s mostly when I’m completely alone in my studio. My studio is in this old, converted warehouse building, so it has these really high ceilings and I have these massive industrial metal shelves right in the middle to divide the space between my wet materials and my drying racks, because you really have to keep the dust away from the drying oils, you know? 

Anyway, sometimes, when it’s just me and it's perfectly quiet, I’ll hear... well, I hear this woman. She’s just quietly commenting on things. It’s always coming from right behind those heavy shelves. At first, I thought maybe it was a neighbor, you know, sound traveling through the old vents? But it’s so close, like she’s standing just on the other side of the racks, just murmuring these quiet little observations about what I'm doing. 

And then there are the smells, too. I’ll be working on an unfinished canvas—just using standard oils and mediums, nothing unusual—but suddenly there’s this overwhelming smell of hot metal right next to the piece. Like... like a soldering iron left on too long, or an overheated radiator. I don't even do metalwork! But it’s so incredibly strong and specific, right there next to the easel. 

And both of these things—the woman’s voice, that burning metal smell—they feel so completely, undeniably real. I mean, I’ll literally put my palette down, wipe my hands on my apron, and walk all the way around the shelves to see who managed to get into my space, or I'll go sniffing around the baseboards and checking the electrical outlets because I'm terrified the wiring is catching fire. I do a full sweep of the room. But every single time I check... there’s just nothing. Nobody is there. The air is totally clear. It’s just me. But in the moment, before I check, I swear to you, it is as real as you sitting across from me right now. It really makes you second-guess your own senses, you know? Because I rely on my senses for my work, so when they do that... it's just very strange.
Do these episodes of tangled thoughts and unusual connections happen all the time, or do they come and go?

Well, gosh, that’s... that’s actually a really tough question to answer. I’m not entirely sure? I mean, trying to track time and patterns is already a bit of a challenge for me, just because of how my life is structured. As a full-time artist, you know, I don’t have that standard nine-to-five schedule where you can easily measure your days against a clock or a set routine. Some days I’m in the studio from six in the morning until midnight, just completely lost in the process, mixing oils and stretching canvases, and time just sort of evaporates. So when I try to look back and figure out if this tangling of my words is happening constantly or if it takes breaks... it all just blends together into this one big wash of experience. 

Sometimes I feel like it must be coming and going, because I’ll look back at my sketchbooks from, say, a few months ago, and my notes in the margins will be perfectly straightforward. Just regular reminders to buy more cadmium red or to call the framer by Tuesday. Completely linear, normal thoughts. But then I’ll look at my notebook from yesterday, and it’s just pages and pages of those intricate webs connecting the pigment density to the cosmos and the financial stuff I was telling you about. 

So I guess that means it fluctuates? But then again, maybe the connections are always there in my head, just sort of simmering under the surface, and I only really notice them when I try to speak or write them down for someone else. Because when I'm just painting, alone, I don't have to explain anything, so I don't realize if my thoughts are tangled or not. The paint just does the talking. So honestly, I really don't know if it's a constant thing or if it comes in waves. I haven't been able to pin down any kind of rhythm or schedule to it at all. It just sort of is what it is when it happens, and I only really become aware of it when someone else points out that they can't understand me.

When you're speaking and your thoughts seem to be jumping from one thing to another, do you feel like you're still making sense and that there's a logical connection between your ideas, even if others don't understand it?

Oh, absolutely. To me, it makes perfect, crystal-clear sense. It's actually... well, it's the whole reason I came in to see you in the first place, to be honest. Because it’s started really affecting my professional life and my livelihood. 

Like, I’ll be sitting down to write my artist statements—which, you know, are already notoriously difficult to write, because trying to translate a purely visual medium into text is a massive challenge on its own—but I’ll be writing those, or I'll be typing up client notes for a new private commission, or even just sitting in planning meetings with gallery directors, and I think I'm being incredibly articulate. I feel like I'm laying out this brilliant, cohesive vision. But apparently, my artist statements, my client notes, and even what I say in meetings have started jumping from discussing the physical textures of the paint directly to the financial budgets for the exhibition, and then straight into these deep, secret meanings behind the materials. 

And to me, the line between those things is so obvious! The rough texture of the raw linen obviously dictates the budget, which obviously reveals the secret meaning of the whole collection and how society values raw materials. It’s a completely logical, straight progression in my head. I can see the bridge connecting all of it perfectly. But then I'll look around the meeting table, and everyone is just staring at me with these blank, uncomfortable faces. They keep telling me they can’t follow what I’m trying to explain. They'll literally stop me and say, "Wait, how did we get from palette knives to the quarterly budget and secret codes?" 

And I have to sit there and realize that they literally cannot see the connections that are right in front of them. It’s incredibly frustrating, because I feel like I'm handing them this beautifully wrapped, intricate package of ideas, and they just look at it like it's a pile of tangled string. So, yes, to me it's completely logical and everything is perfectly linked, but since people keep telling me they can't follow my explanations anymore, I knew I had to come in. Because if I can't communicate with my galleries or my clients, I don't know how I'm supposed to keep my studio running, you know?
When you're speaking and your thoughts seem to be jumping from one thing to another, do you feel like there's a central idea or theme that ties everything together?

Well, a central theme... I mean, I suppose there is, deep down at the very bottom of it all, but honestly? It’s not so much about a neat little theme tying it all together with a bow as it is about the... the sheer velocity of everything. It’s like my brain is just hitting the accelerator and the brakes have completely given out. 

Because my thoughts, they just move so incredibly fast. It’s not a gentle wandering from one topic to the next, like taking a stroll through a garden. It’s more like... before I can even finish articulating one single idea in my head, everything else just aggressively stacks right on top of it. Like, I’ll be standing there, maybe just trying to focus on prepping a canvas, and suddenly I’ve got the visual images of what the finished piece will look like, and then a dozen different working titles for the entire exhibition, and then the highly specific, incredibly dry language for this state arts council grant I’m trying to finish by Friday, and the exact mixing ratios for the colors—like whether the shadows need a cool ultramarine or a warmer cobalt—and then fragments of conversations I had with the gallery director last week... 

And all of these things—the images, the titles, the grant language, the colors, the conversations—they just all stack on top of each other in a fraction of a second. Boom, boom, boom. It all piles up before I can even finish that first original thought about prepping the canvas. 

So, if there is a central idea, it just gets completely buried under this absolute avalanche of information. I can’t even get to the end of a thought before the next ten things have crashed into it. It’s just this massive, high-speed collision of every aspect of my life and my work all happening at the exact same moment. So when I'm speaking and it sounds to other people like I'm jumping around or losing the thread, it's really just me trying to physically keep up with this massive, heavy stack of ideas that’s racing through my mind all at once. It’s exhausting, frankly, because I’m trying to voice a hundred miles an hour of thought into a ten mile an hour conversation, you know?
Do you find that your rapid thought connections and jumping between ideas happen more often when you're exposed to certain environments, people, or activities?

Environments or activities... gosh, yes, absolutely. It’s funny you ask that because I was just thinking about how my physical space interacts with all of this. You know, my studio is in this old, repurposed industrial warehouse building—which is fantastic for the sheer square footage and the huge windows, but it has all these little quirks. And I’ve noticed that this whole jumping around of my thoughts gets incredibly intense when I have to sit down and do the administrative side of being an artist. 

Like, when I try to write a proposal—especially that state arts council grant I mentioned earlier, which requires so much rigid, structured thinking—it's like my brain just absolutely rebels against it. I'll be sitting at my desk, trying so hard to focus on the budget narrative or the project timeline, and the absolute tiniest thing in the room will completely hijack my attention. It could literally just be the buzz of a fluorescent light overhead. Or I'll catch a shadow moving on the wall from the streetlamps and the cars outside, or I'll just glance down and read one single line in an old notebook I have sitting open on the corner of my desk... and that's it. I'm gone. 

Any of those things can pull me completely off task and send me into something completely different. I’ll go from trying to write a professional proposal to suddenly spending four hours researching the electrical grid of the city because of that buzzing light, or I'll start tearing apart my studio trying to build a whole new sculpture out of wire that mimics the exact shape of the shadow I just saw. Or that one line in the notebook will make me pull out twenty other notebooks to trace the origin of that specific word, and before I know it, the sun is coming up, the proposal is totally forgotten, and I'm surrounded by this massive, chaotic new project. It’s like my environment becomes this minefield, and the second I try to focus on a quiet activity like writing, every little sensory detail just yanks me into a totally new, massive web of ideas.
Do you ever feel like you're unusually energetic or restless, like you can't slow down?

Oh, energetic doesn't even begin to cover it. It’s more like... it’s like I have this massive, industrial motor humming inside my chest and someone just completely ripped the off-switch out of the wall. I get these surges where I literally just cannot stop moving. 

I’ll just get these bursts, these massive waves of pure, unfiltered drive. Like, out of nowhere, I’ll suddenly take on three different exhibition proposals all at the exact same time—which is absolute madness, you know, because just writing one proposal takes weeks of careful planning. But I’ll commit to three, and then, right in the middle of trying to juggle all that paperwork, I’ll decide that the spatial flow of my workspace is completely stifling my creative energy, so I'll start physically dragging these massive, heavy wooden worktables and metal shelving units across the concrete floor to completely reorganize the studio. 

And it doesn't stop there, it just bleeds into the night. I won't even realize the sun went down. I’ll just sit there and sketch all night long, filling up sketchbook after sketchbook, page after page, until my hand is literally cramping up and covered in graphite. And because I'm up and my blood is just buzzing with all this momentum, I’ll start drafting and sending out these incredibly long emails to curators and gallery directors at, like, 3:30 in the morning. Which, in hindsight, I know probably looks incredibly erratic and unprofessional when they open their inboxes the next day, but in the moment, I just can't wait. The ideas have to go out right then and there. 

And then, before I even hear back from a single one of those curators, I’ll just start pulling out my most expensive rolls of raw linen and lumber and I'll start cutting materials for pieces I haven’t even budgeted yet! Like, I have absolutely no idea how I'm going to pay for the rest of the month's supplies or rent, but I'm just slicing into the canvas with my shears because I have to make the piece a reality right that exact second. It's just this relentless, physical need to keep moving, keep producing, keep doing, doing, doing... and I literally just cannot force myself to slow down and take a breath.
Do you ever feel like you're not needing as much sleep as you used to, yet you still have plenty of energy?

Oh, sleep... sleep has just become this completely secondary thing, almost like a nuisance, honestly. Because, like I was just saying about being up all night sketching or moving those massive worktables around? Well, eventually, usually around, I don't know, maybe five in the morning when the sun is just starting to come up and the light in the studio gets that really flat, grayish-blue quality... I might finally just collapse. 

I have this little vintage velvet sofa in the corner of my workspace—it's this gorgeous deep emerald green, absolutely terrible for your back, but I just crash right there in my clothes with graphite still all over my hands. And you would think, logically, after doing all that heavy lifting and having my brain running at absolute top speed for twenty hours straight, that I would be dead to the world for at least a full day. But no. It's the exact opposite. I can sleep for literally just two or three hours after working late like that, and then my eyes will just snap open. Boom. Wide awake. 

And the crazy thing is, I don't wake up groggy or dragging or dreading the day, which is how I normally would be if I only got a couple of hours of rest, you know? Usually, I'm a complete zombie without my eight hours, I wouldn't even be able to mix a proper color wash or hold a thought in my head. But when this is happening? I wake up feeling so incredibly bright and just... ready to keep going. It’s like those two or three hours were a full, deep hibernation, and my body is just humming, completely refreshed. I just hop right off that terrible little sofa and I'm instantly back at a hundred percent, not tired the way I normally would be in the slightest, just completely energized and ready to dive right back into the canvas.
Have you ever had a period of time where you felt extremely happy or irritable, and your thoughts were racing, and you had a lot of energy, that lasted for several days or longer?

Oh, absolutely. Yes, for stretches—sometimes a week or even longer—it’s exactly like that. I’ll go into these periods where I just feel completely lit up from the inside out. It’s this glowing, buzzing sensation, and I feel almost completely unstoppable. Like, during those days, I am absolutely convinced that every single idea that crosses my mind is just pure brilliance. I'll be looking at a piece of scrap metal or a smear of paint on the floor and think I've just solved the entire puzzle of contemporary spatial design, you know? It’s this euphoric, expansive high where everything I touch is just gold and I’m operating on this entirely different, elevated plane of existence. 

But the really tricky part—and this is what makes it so complicated to navigate—is that it’s not just sunshine and happiness. Because I’m running at such a high frequency, the wire is pulled incredibly tight. So, I’ll be in the middle of this unstoppable streak, feeling like an absolute genius, and then I'll be working with a collaborator—maybe another artist I'm doing a joint show with, or someone helping me fabricate a heavy mount—and they’ll make a small comment. Just the tiniest, most innocuous thing. Like, maybe they suggest adjusting a lighting angle by two degrees, or they ask a simple question about a measurement. And instead of just answering them normally, I will completely snap. 

And I mean snap in a way that feels so much bigger than the situation actually warrants. It’s like this sudden, white-hot flash of intense irritation, and I’ll just bite their head off because, in that moment, their tiny little question feels like this massive, insulting roadblock to my brilliant vision. I get so intensely defensive and irritable over absolutely nothing. So it's this exhausting combination where I'm soaring, feeling like the greatest creator alive, but if anyone interrupts my flow or questions even a fraction of what I'm doing, I just explode at them. And that whole dynamic, the soaring and the snapping, will just keep going and going for days on end without letting up.
Have you ever had a period where your extremely high energy and racing thoughts lasted for several days without stopping?

Oh, absolutely, yes. Days at a time, easily. It’s like... well, you asked about the racing thoughts, and it's honestly the most intense part of the whole experience, even more than the physical energy, I think. Because my mind just completely takes off, and I mean, it moves *so* incredibly fast. It's not just one train of thought, it's like a ten-lane highway and every single car is going two hundred miles an hour. 

Before I can even finish processing one single idea, another one just slams right into it. Like, I’ll be standing there in the studio, and suddenly I have these vivid, massive images of a new installation flashing in my head, and then right on top of that, I'm coming up with the exact exhibition titles, and then suddenly I'm mentally drafting the specific, highly technical grant language I need to apply for funding for it... and then that gets completely buried under this overwhelming flood of just... colors. Specific palettes, like cadmium red and raw sienna just splashing over everything else in my mind's eye. And while all of that is happening, I'll be replaying past conversations I had with gallery owners, or anticipating future conversations I need to have with fabricators, and it all just... it all just stacks on top of each other. 

It just piles up so fast that I literally cannot finish one single, coherent idea before ten more have completely crushed it. And this won't just be for a busy afternoon. Oh, no. This will go on for three, four, five days straight, just this relentless, chaotic slideshow in my brain that I can't turn off or even pause. It's like I'm trying to catch rain in a sieve, you know? Because there's so much happening up there, so much brilliant material, but it's just moving at warp speed, stacking and stacking and stacking, day after day, from the moment I wake up—if I even sleep—until the next morning. I'll even try to write it all down in my notebooks, but my hand just physically cannot keep up with the grant language and the titles and the colors and the dialogue, it's just... a complete avalanche of thought.
Have you ever had a period where you felt like you were on top of the world, and nothing could bring you down, that lasted for several days or longer?

Oh, absolutely. It's exactly like that. When I get into these spaces, these stretches of days where everything is just clicking... I don't just feel good, I feel completely untouchable. It's like, at my most charged up, I'll look at the work I'm doing and I truly, genuinely feel like I am about to completely change how everyone understands installation art. Like, the entire paradigm of the art world is going to shift because of what I'm doing right there in my studio. 

And usually, you know, as an artist, you constantly have all these heavy, practical constraints weighing on you. You have to worry about gallery space, and who is going to pay for the raw materials, and whether you have the right CV or the right connections to even get a curator to look at your portfolio. It's exhausting. But when I'm in that elevated zone, for those days on end, all of that just completely evaporates. I'll be planning these massive, multi-room sensory experiences, and it just feels like normal limits—like funding, or time constraints, or even my own level of professional experience—they just don't really apply to me. 

Because why would they? In my head, the vision is so pure and so revolutionary that of course the money will just magically appear, or of course I can build a twenty-foot steel armature by myself in three days, even though I've never welded anything quite that size before. I just get this overwhelming sense of destiny, I guess you could call it. Like I'm just floating above all the red tape and the logistics that drag everyone else down. I remember once I spent literally four days mapping out a concept for an exhibition that would require flooding an entire warehouse floor with dyed water, and I didn't pause for a single second to consider how impossible the insurance or the plumbing would be, because I just *knew* I was operating on a level that transcended all of those mundane details. It's just this absolute, unshakable certainty that I am the exception to every single rule, and nothing can convince me otherwise when I'm riding that wave.
Do you ever feel like your incredibly high energy and racing thoughts make it difficult for you to distinguish between what's real and what's not?

Yeah... yeah, it does. It gets incredibly blurry, actually. Because when I am in those really, really charged-up work periods—the ones where I'm just taking on way, way too much and pushing myself to the absolute physical limit... I mean, I'll be sleeping maybe an hour or two a night, if that, just subsisting on cold coffee and the pure adrenaline of the work. And when I get to that point, where the energy is just vibrating through my teeth and my thoughts are moving that fast, the boundary between what's actually happening and what my brain is... constructing... it just completely dissolves. 

Like, I'll be standing there in the studio, and you know, it's a workspace, the floor is covered in years of accumulated mess. But I'll look down at these random stains on the concrete—spilled turpentine, or a weird splatter of gesso, or just watermarks from a leaky pipe—and suddenly, I am absolutely sure that they aren't just accidents. I'll become completely convinced that the shapes of the stains are actually sending me highly specific instructions. Like a schematic or a code that only I can read, telling me exactly how to position a sculpture or what materials to fuse together. 

And it bleeds into everything else, too. I'll sit down at my laptop to check my messages, and I'll be reading these totally mundane emails from, like, a hardware supplier or a gallery intern, but certain words will just... jump out at me. They'll seem to hold this immense, hidden weight. I'll read a sentence about a shipping delay or an invoice, and I'll just know, with absolute certainty, that those specific email phrases are actually covert instructions guiding my artistic direction. Like someone or something is trying to send me a secret message through the text, telling me what I have to do next. 

And then... the most disorienting part is that I'll start hearing her. While I'm frantically trying to decode the stains and the emails, I'll sometimes hear this woman's voice, right there in the room with me. Just... commenting on my work. Critiquing what I'm doing in the studio, making little observations about my technique or the scale of the piece or the lighting. And it sounds so real, echoing off the walls, that in that high-energy state, I don't even stop to question why there's a woman speaking to me in a locked room at four in the morning. I just sort of weave it all into the grand, unstoppable momentum of the project. I just accept the instructions and the voice as part of the brilliance, and it's only way, way later that I realize how far removed from reality I actually was.
Do you ever feel extremely down or depressed after one of these high-energy periods ends?

Well, honestly... no, not really. I wouldn't call it depressed at all. It's actually kind of strange, because I know people always talk about, like, a crash? But for me, when that incredible momentum finally runs out, it's... it's really just a physical thing. I don't get that heavy, dark, hopeless feeling that I think you're asking about. 

It's more like... well, imagine you've been running a marathon at a dead sprint, right? When you finally stop, you aren't sad that you stopped, your body just literally cannot hold you up anymore. So my brain will finally quiet down, and I'll just kind of... look around the studio. And the studio is usually an absolute disaster zone by that point. I mean, we're talking empty coffee cups stacked on top of expensive power tools, hardened resin on the floor, sketchpads just completely filled with those frantic notes I mentioned earlier, just scattered everywhere. And I'll stand there in the middle of it all, and I just feel this immense, overwhelming physical exhaustion. Like my bones are suddenly made of lead. 

I'll usually just go back to my apartment and sleep for, I don't know, maybe fourteen or fifteen hours straight. Just completely dead to the world. And when I wake up, I don't feel down or tearful or anything like that. I just feel... quiet. The ten-lane highway in my head is just empty again. I might feel a little bit daunted by the massive amount of cleanup I have to do, because, you know, dried acrylic ruins the good brushes if you don't wash them out, and I always, always forget to wash them when I'm in that zone. But emotionally? No, I don't drop into a depression. I just sort of reset back to my normal self. Just a very, very tired version of my normal self, trying to figure out how to organize all the chaotic work I just produced over the last five days.
Do you usually feel sad or empty after these periods of extremely high energy and rapid thoughts come to an end?

Like I... like I was just saying a second ago, no, I really don't. I know you're asking again, and I get it, maybe it's super common for people to have this huge emotional crash where they feel terrible, but for me, it's just exactly what I was describing with that physical exhaustion. 

When you use the word "empty," I mean... sure, my head feels a little empty, but not in a sad, hollow, despairing kind of way. It’s just quiet. It's literally just that my internal battery is at zero percent. I don't sit around crying or feeling like life is meaningless. Honestly, after I wake up from sleeping those fourteen or fifteen hours, the main thing I feel isn't sadness, it's just extreme, ravenous hunger. Because, you know, I haven't been eating properly for days, just living off adrenaline and maybe some stale crackers I found in my studio drawer. 

So I'll usually just order a massive amount of takeout—like, an absurd amount of Pad Thai or something—and I'll just sit on my couch in my sweatpants. And I'm not depressed while I'm sitting there. I'm just chewing my noodles, staring into space, and mentally calculating how much heavy-duty solvent I need to buy to scrape all the hardened gesso off my workspace. There's no dark cloud that comes over me, no emotional void. The engine just completely stops running hot, and I just have to wait for it to cool down and refuel before I can go back to being my regular self. So, yeah, no sadness or emptiness in my soul. Just a lot of sleeping, eating, and eventually sweeping up the mess.
Do you usually feel sad or empty after these periods of extremely high energy and rapid thoughts come to an end?

I... I feel like maybe I'm not explaining myself right, because you keep asking me this same thing. Or maybe you're just checking to see if my answer changes? But really, honestly, no. Like I've been saying, I do not get sad. I don't get empty. 

I mean, I get why you're digging at this. I know there's this whole cliché, right? The tortured artist trope. Like, you fly too close to the sun, you make all this wild, brilliant work, and then you crash down into this deep, dark abyss of despair and emptiness and you can't get out of bed because life is just this meaningless void. People love that narrative. But that is just... that's not my reality at all. 

When the energy stops, it just stops. It’s literally like unplugging a television set. The screen goes black, but the TV isn't sad about it, you know? It’s just off. I’ll spend that first day awake just doing the most boring, grounding things imaginable to recover. I'll take a shower that lasts like forty-five minutes because I'm scrubbing literal layers of dried paint and sweat and dust off my skin. And I'll just stand there under the hot water, and my mind is completely blank. But not empty like a void that hurts, just... blank. Peaceful, almost. 

And then I'll sit in my living room, and I'll watch, I don't know, a documentary about deep-sea fish or something equally mindless, just letting the narrator's voice wash over me while I try to untangle the giant knots in my hair. There's no crying. There's no feeling like I'm worthless or that the world is bleak. It's just a transition back to being a regular twenty-nine-year-old who has to pay rent and buy groceries and do laundry. So, yeah, I really, truly don't get sad or empty. I just get physically drained. I really hope that makes sense this time, because I don't think I can find another way to describe just being intensely, deeply tired.
Do you think that after these periods of extremely high energy, you might be entering into a depressive state without realizing it?

I... okay, I see what you're doing. You're wondering if maybe I just lack the self-awareness to recognize it when it happens. Which, you know, is a fair question, I guess. Because people can be completely blind to their own patterns. Like my friend Sarah, she always dates these guys who are emotionally unavailable, and she genuinely thinks she's just "unlucky," but everyone else can clearly see she's seeking them out. So I understand why you'd ask if I'm just, like, missing the signs of a depression.

But... no. I really, truly don't think I am. Because I know what depression looks like. I've seen people go through it. And I am very, very in tune with my own body and my own mind. You kind of have to be when you're an artist, right? You have to know where your emotional baseline is so you can pull from it for your work. And when I come down from one of those intense, high-energy weeks, I'm not slipping into some sneaky, invisible depression.
